sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Credential gatekeeping and vague culture-fit judgments were among the clearest advancement barriers DSD staff described. Each stage of hiring is a decision with an owner, so each can be changed.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Stage 1. Test essential duties and remove excessive credential barriers. Write down what the job actually requires people to do. For each degree, years-of-experience, or licensure requirement, ask whether it predicts that work or stands in for it. Name credible alternatives such as lived experience, community work, or demonstrated skill.

Stage 2. Expand accessible outreach beyond familiar networks. Post where people outside your usual circles will see it, in plain language, with the salary range and the accommodation statement visible. Ask community partners to share it and tell them how to reach a human.

Stage 3. Use structured review and job-relevant rubrics. Screen every application against the same written criteria tied to the work. Record the reason for each decision so the process can be checked later.

Stage 4. Normalize accommodations without forcing disclosure. Offer accommodation for every stage in the same sentence you use for scheduling. Make the offer to everyone so no one has to identify as disabled to receive it.

Stage 5. Use structured interviews and avoid vague culture fit. Ask every candidate the same core questions tied to the rubric. Replace culture fit with the specific behaviors the team needs, such as working across difference or explaining a decision to a family.

Stage 6. Make bias reflection part of deliberation. Before deciding, have the panel name what impressed them and check it against the rubric. Ask what the panel might be rewarding that is not job related, such as fluency, confidence, or familiarity.
Stage 7. Provide a transparent offer and onboarding. Explain how the salary was set and what advancement requires. Plan the first weeks so a new person knows who to ask and how decisions get made.

Stage 8. Examine stage-by-stage outcomes and improve the process. With your HR partner, look at who applied, who advanced at each stage, and who was hired, at a level that protects small groups. Change the stage where people drop out.

What this is not. This is practice guidance. Selection procedures, classification, labor agreements, and civil-rights obligations are governed by Human Resources, labor relations, and law. Bring this plan to those partners rather than around them.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Federal guidance on employee selection expects employers to examine procedures that produce adverse impact and to have evidence that they are job related. This check helps you ask those questions before a posting goes out, without removing qualifications the work really needs.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Question 1. What part of the work does this requirement predict? Write the specific tasks. If you cannot name them, the requirement may be a proxy.
Question 2. What evidence do we have that it predicts that work? Consider whether current strong performers all meet it, and whether people without it have done the work well elsewhere.

Question 3. Who does this requirement screen out? Think about communities, first-generation professionals, people who built skills outside formal education, and people with disabilities who took different paths.
Question 4. What alternative shows the same ability? Consider a work sample, a portfolio, described experience, a certification, or a structured question in the interview.
Question 5. Who reviewed and signed off? Note the hiring manager, the HR partner, and, where practice calls for it, the Equity Director. Keep the reasoning with the posting.

Do not remove qualifications categorically. Some work requires a license or a specific credential. The point is to know what the work genuinely requires and which credible forms of experience demonstrate capability.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: DSD staff described inconsistent recognition of work and lived experience, classification and pay concerns, and unclear pathways. These are patterns, not individual failings, and they respond to practice.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: What you can change now. Say out loud what advancement requires in your unit and write it down. Rotate visible assignments deliberately instead of by who is closest. Hold a career conversation with every person, not only the ones who ask. Sponsor people into rooms where decisions are made, not only mentor them about how rooms work.

What needs a partner. Classification questions, reclassification requests, pay equity reviews, and anything governed by a labor agreement go to Human Resources and labor relations. Bring the pattern you noticed and the people affected in general terms, not a case for one person.

What to watch for. Reverse mentoring can be valuable, but it should not become unpaid equity labor for staff from underrepresented communities. Development plans should not be treated as proof of competence or as a hidden record.

Questions to ask yourself. Who on the team has had a stretch assignment in the last year, and how did that come to be? Who has been told plainly what the next step requires? Whose work is visible to leadership, and whose is not?

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: People who are new to an organization's informal rules often get plenty of advice and very little sponsorship. Advancement usually depends on the second.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Mentoring. Regular conversations about how decisions are made, what the next role requires, and how to prepare. Useful, and usually not enough on its own.

Sponsorship. A leader names a person for a stretch assignment, a panel, a project lead role, or a promotion conversation, and stands behind that recommendation. Sponsorship is where advancement actually happens. Track, at a level that protects individuals, who gets sponsored.

Reverse mentoring. A leader learns from a staff member whose experience differs from theirs. It works when the leader asks for it, the staff member chooses it, the time is recognized as work, and the leader acts on what they learn. It fails when it becomes a standing expectation placed on staff from underrepresented communities.
A practical start. Ask each leader in your unit to name one person they will sponsor this quarter and for what. Review the list for who is missing.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Exit patterns arrive too late to act on. Stay conversations surface barriers while there is still time, and they signal that a person's experience matters.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Before. Tell the person what the conversation is and is not. It is not a performance review and nothing said will be written into a record. Offer to hold it in whatever setting works for them.

During. Ask open questions. What do you look forward to here? What would make you consider leaving? What have you wanted to say that you have not had a chance to? What would you change about how work is assigned or recognized? Listen more than you speak.
After. Choose one thing you can change and tell the person what it is. If a pattern appears across several conversations, take the pattern, not the names, to your leadership or Equity Director.

Boundaries. If the conversation raises a complaint about a named person, harassment, or discrimination, stop and connect the person to the confidential channel. Do not investigate and do not record it here.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Equity cannot be confined to awareness content. This canvas turns it into the working steps of an actual decision while the decision can still change.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Step 1. Clarify the decision. What exactly is being decided, by whom, and by when? What is already fixed and what is still open?
Step 2. Identify affected people. Who benefits, who carries the burden, and who is missing from the room? Consider community, language, disability, age, place, and the people who deliver the service.
Step 3. Examine evidence. What do we know by community, language, disability, and place? What do people who use the service say? What does the evidence not show?
Step 4. Name assumptions and risks. What are we assuming about people's access, time, documents, technology, or trust? What could go wrong for the people with the least margin?
Step 5. Compare options. Lay out at least two alternatives and compare who each helps and burdens. Include the option of not proceeding.
Step 6. Choose accountable owners. Who owns each part of implementation and each follow-up? Name people, not units.
Step 7. Define accessible implementation. How will people learn about the change, in which languages and formats, with what human alternative? What burden can still be removed?
Step 8. Schedule follow-up. When will you look at what happened, what will you look at, and who will report back to the people who gave input?
Any figures used as examples in training materials are illustrations, not DSD evidence. Use the real data owners for real numbers.

paragraphs: Contracts decide who delivers services and how. Adding equity language after award changes little. Procurement and grants offices own the rules; equity professionals help shape the questions in time.

paragraphs: Before the solicitation. Who will the service reach, and in which languages and formats? Which communities have providers that could deliver it but rarely win awards, and why? What accessibility requirements apply to the deliverables?

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Equity in disability services is inseparable from disability rights. A redesign that adds steps, removes choice, or assumes incapacity can be inaccessible and inequitable at once.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Person-centered planning. The person directs the plan; the system organizes around their goals, relationships, and preferences. Ask how a process lets the person lead rather than respond.
Supported decision-making. People have the right to make their own decisions with support they choose. Ask whether a process assumes incapacity or offers support.
LifeCourse. A framework for thinking about a good life across a lifetime, using the person's vision and a mix of supports. Useful for planning conversations; it is one framework among several.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: The most common harm in engagement is asking for input that cannot change anything. Naming the level of influence protects trust and tells people what their time is worth.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Inform. You tell people what is happening and why. Appropriate when the decision is already made. Say so.
Consult. You ask for input and decide. Appropriate when choices are open and you will explain what you did with the input.
Involve. People work with you throughout and their concerns shape the options. Appropriate when the decision affects them directly and the timeline allows.
Collaborate. People share in developing options and in the decision. Appropriate when you can share authority and want the result to be owned together.
Co-design. People with lived experience lead the design with you. Appropriate when the service is theirs and you are prepared to change how it works.

Assign an owner for the ongoing relationship.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Meetings are where participation is won or lost. Camera use, eye contact, speed, and silence are not universal evidence of engagement, and treating them that way excludes people.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Before. Send the purpose, agenda, and materials at least a few working days ahead in an accessible format. Include the accommodation sentence in every invitation: tell us what you need to take part fully. Turn captions on by default. Check the room or platform for physical, sensory, and technology access.

During. Open with the purpose and how decisions will be made. Offer several ways to contribute: speaking, writing in advance, writing in chat, or following up afterward. Rotate who opens and who summarizes. Read written input aloud so it carries the same weight. Watch who is speaking and who is not, and notice positional power in the room. Slow down when interpretation or captioning is in use.

When harm occurs. Name it, pause, and make repair the responsibility of the person with more power in the room. Do not ask the person harmed to explain or to fix it. Follow up privately with the people involved.
Ending. State each decision, its owner, and its date. Say what happens to input that was not used.
After. Send accessible notes with decisions and owners in the same channels people used. Ask how the meeting worked for people and change the next one.
Notice periods, captioning accuracy claims, and accommodation instructions should follow your division's current accessibility guidance. Check with your accessibility lead.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Start with the answer. Put the main point in the first sentence and the action in the first paragraph.

Test it. Read it aloud. Ask a colleague what they would do after reading it. If they are unsure, the writing is not finished.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: The idea. Coined in legal scholarship to describe how discrimination against Black women was invisible to claims that looked at race or sex alone. The same pattern appears in services: a deaf Somali elder's experience is not the sum of three separate briefs.
In data. Ask the data owner what can be disaggregated by more than one category with small-group protection. Where numbers are too small, use qualitative evidence and say so.
In engagement. Ask who is missing at the intersections, and plan access for people who face more than one barrier at once, such as interpretation and captioning together.
In design. Test a process against the person with the least margin: the person who needs an interpreter, an accessible format, transportation, and a daytime alternative all at once.
In the workplace. Advancement barriers and climate problems land differently on people who hold more than one marginalized identity. Ask, do not assume.

body: The idea. Coined in legal scholarship to describe how discrimination against Black women was invisible to claims that looked at race or sex alone. The same pattern appears in services: a deaf Somali elder's experience is not the sum of three separate briefs.
In data. Ask the data owner what can be disaggregated by more than one category with small-group protection. Where numbers are too small, use qualitative evidence and say so.
In engagement. Ask who is missing at the intersections, and plan access for people who face more than one barrier at once, such as interpretation and captioning together.
In design. Test a process against the person with the least margin: the person who needs an interpreter, an accessible format, transportation, and a daytime alternative all at once.
In the workplace. Advancement barriers and climate problems land differently on people who hold more than one marginalized identity. Ask, do not assume.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Invented targets, composite scores without validation, and individualized learning surveillance destroy trust and prove nothing. Good measurement is possible and protects people.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Two different questions. Does the platform work: can people find, use, and apply material? Does the program improve equity practice or outcomes: are decisions, services, and workplace patterns changing? Measure both, separately.
Logic model. Inputs and activities, outputs, outcomes, and impact. Write what you expect to change and by when before you measure.
Baselines first. No causal claim without a baseline. If there is no baseline, say so and start one.
Mixed methods. Numbers show patterns; people's accounts show why. Use both, and give qualitative evidence equal standing.

Disaggregate with protection. By community, language, disability, and place where the data allows. Set the smallest group you will report, and suppress below it. Ask the data owner about denominators.
Protect private learning. Learning, reflection, Ask, and practice paths are private. Report only combined totals that cannot identify anyone, and never use them for supervision or evaluation.
Never use assessment results as performance data. Intercultural assessments and similar instruments describe development; they are not scores of competence and must not enter personnel decisions.
State the limits. Every report says what the evidence does not show. That sentence is what makes the rest trustworthy.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Disclosure is a cost. Many staff will not identify as disabled to a supervisor or a program, so pathway design cannot depend on knowing who is disabled. It has to be accessible to everyone and honest about what leadership roles actually require.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: Engagement without forced disclosure. Work through anonymous aggregate listening, disability employee resource groups, and trusted intermediaries, with small-group suppression in any reporting. Ask about the pathway, not the person: what does it take to be seen as ready for a lead role here, who explains it, and what happens when someone asks for an accommodation during a stretch assignment or interview.
Close the loop publicly. Disabled staff in particular have watched accessibility promises go unfunded. Report what changed, what did not, and who owns the next step.

Examine the pipeline stage by stage: nomination to leadership programs, selection for visible projects, acting assignments, interview formats, and promotion outcomes. Disability is often absent from disaggregated workforce data, so the first finding may be that the organization cannot see the pattern at all. Say so.

Test the job-relatedness of leadership criteria. Executive presence, quick verbal response, travel, long hours, and always-on availability screen out many disabled staff and are rarely tied to what leaders actually do.

Look for the accommodation cliff. Accommodations that exist for the current role are often lost during a rotation, a leadership cohort, or an interview process because nobody owns them across the transition. Name an owner for accommodations across every transition.

Sponsorship, not just mentoring. Mentoring gives advice; sponsorship puts someone's name forward. Pair disabled staff who want it with sponsors who hold decision power, and track at the program level whether sponsorship leads to assignments.
Reverse mentoring, where disabled staff advise leaders on what accessible leadership looks like, with compensation or recognized time and never as a standing expectation.

Accessible leadership programs by default: materials in advance, captioning, flexible participation formats, no timed or drag-based activities, and accommodations carried across every cohort event. The State of Minnesota Emerging Leaders Institute run by Minnesota Management and Budget is the verified public program; DHS-level pathways should be reviewed against the same standard.
Transparent pathway maps that say what a lead or supervisor role requires, which experiences count, and how to get them, so advancement does not depend on informal networks.
Structured leadership interviews with rubrics tied to the work, accommodations offered without asking why, and panel preparation on disability bias.
Stay conversations that ask about growth and access together, and exit patterns reviewed at an appropriate level.

Boundaries this program keeps. No guessing about disability: the program never guesses who is disabled from behavior, accommodation history, or participation. No individual tracking: private learning and reflection stay private, and program-level measures use aggregates with suppression. Accommodation requests, complaints, and personnel decisions go to the confidential channels, never into this program.
Who owns what. ADA and accommodation decisions belong to Human Resources and the accommodation process. Pathway design belongs to leadership and the equity practice. Take each to its owner.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Leadership criteria are rarely written down and rarely tested. The ones that live in people's heads tend to reward a narrow style of presence and stamina rather than the work of leading.

sections.heading: What to know
paragraphs: List every criterion actually used. Include the unwritten ones: who gets called confident, who is seen as ready, who is invited to present.

For each criterion, write the leadership work it predicts. Decisions made, people developed, conflicts resolved, plans delivered, communities served. If you cannot connect it to that work, it is a proxy.

Ask who each criterion screens out. Quick verbal response screens out people who process or communicate differently. Travel and long hours screen out people with energy, mobility, or care constraints. Always-on availability screens out most people with a disability and many without one.
Replace proxies with observable leadership behaviors and give people several ways to show them: written work, a portfolio, a structured conversation, a work sample with time to prepare.
Offer accommodation for every stage in the same sentence you use for scheduling, to everyone, without asking why.
Prepare the panel on disability bias before the interviews, and use a written rubric applied the same way to everyone.
Record who reviewed the criteria: leadership, the HR partner, and the Equity Director. Keep the reasoning with the pathway map.
